newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Europe's cartel busters buzzing with activity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Europe's cartel busters buzzing with activity.

text.p: Price-fixing companies beware! Although the European Commission appears to have gone quiet, its top cartel buster warns that his department has never been so busy.
The Commission has not made any spectacular announcements since 1994 when it adopted record fines on cement and cardboard companies found guilty of practices restrictive of fair competition.
But European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert warned recently that a series of decisions were in the pipeline and a senior EU source said a "few cases" were indeed expected this year.

"We've rarely had so many investigations going on at the same time," the anti-trust source said, adding that it takes the Commission an average of three years to conduct the probes, but this could well stretch to four or five years.
DAWN RAIDS ON SUSPECTS

Cartel investigations are the most challenging task performed by the Commission's competition directorate general, better known as DGIV, as companies are unlikely to confess any wrongdoing and documentary evidence is difficult to obtain.
The bulk of the documents is normally seized in surprise "dawn raids" of suspected companies' offices.

EU inspectors recently raided the European offices of U.S. agribusiness giant Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) and Japan's Kyowa Hakko Kogyo on suspicion of price-fixing in amino acids, used as additives in livestock feed.

There is a story about the minutes of a price conspiracy meeting in a Swiss hotel hanging on the window sill of one of the companies searched, but EU inspectors are more likely to return to base laden with thousands of less compromising papers in several languages as cartels usually spread across borders.

Presenting the EU's 1996 competition report at the European Parliament last month, Van Miert gave the example of the confiscation of abundant documents in Swedish -- a language which until very recently nobody in DGIV understood.
Sweden joined the EU in 1994 together with Finland and Austria, considerably contributing to the Commission's competition workload. But Swedish officials swelled DGIV's ranks only later.
WHISTLEBLOWER RULES BEAR FRUIT

The adoption in 1996 of rules encouraging companies to report any cartels in return for immunity from or a reduction in fines is increasingly bearing fruit as demonstrated by the high number of ongoing probes.

Asked whether there had been many whistleblowers the senior official said: "Frankly yes, that was the immediate effect, although we would have preferred that it had the effect of dissuading companies from entering into restrictive agreements altogether".

Japan's Ajinimoto Co, which together with ADM and Kyowa, was charged by the U.S. anti-trust authority last year for fixing the prices of lysine and citric acid, is reported to have cooperated in the EU investigation, although the Commission would not confirm or deny this.
INFORMERS HELP BEAT EURO-COURT CHALLENGES

Help from informers, an idea first used successfully in the United States, will not only facilitate the Commission's work to crack open illegal cartels. It is also expected to help it build up more solid cases to resist challenges in the European Court of Justice.

Commission decisions to impose fines have in the past almost systematically been challenged in the European Court of First Instance, which often criticised the EU executive for lack of respect for procedural rules. This has led to reinforcement of the right to defence at an earlier stage in the investigation procedure.

Article 85 of the Treaty of Rome, the European Union's founding text, gives the Commission the power to ban agreements or concerted practices to fix prices, share markets and limit or control production.
Van Miert told the parliament that his services were currently probing between 14 and 16 suspected cartels. But the senior official said 12 was a more exact figure.
"You should expect a few decisions this year", he said.
In November 1994 the Commission imposed record fines of 248 million European currency units ($280 million) on 33 cement companies for operating a broad market-sharing cartel since 1983.
Earlier the same year, it also fined 19 cardboard firms a total 130 million Ecus ($147 million) for what Van Miert at the time called the "most pernicious" price fixing cartel.

The Commission has been investigating for several years cartel allegations in the steel sector, which has been a target several times before. Current probes focus on the pricing of large tubes used in the oil and the gas industries and on a long-standing practice of adding an "alloy charge" to the price of special steel products.

A decision is also due on another probe into district heating pipes which involves Swiss-Swedish engineering giant Asea Brown Boveri and other companies in the Nordic countries as well as Germany and Austria.
